source.title: Training shallow ReLU networks on noisy data using hinge loss: when do we overfit and is it benign?
source.authors: Erin George; Michael Murray; W. Swartworth; D. Needell

record.file_problem: Full text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper proves that noisy-label fitting and generalization depend on the clean-data margin: it gives benign overfitting, harmful overfitting, and no-overfitting regimes under a restrictive synthetic data model. It refines the broader claim but does not test the listed versions' specific random-label, unstructured-input, or regularization conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theoretical results and simulations concern structured, linearly separable synthetic data with a minority of flipped labels. It does not test completely random labels or random, shuffled, or Gaussian inputs. It does not sweep the corruption fraction from none to all, compare time against clean-label training, or test regularization. The cited Zhang et al. results are prior work and are not extracted as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The study bears on V4's perfect-fitting component through both interpolation and no-overfitting results, and on V6 through its analysis of clean-first training dynamics. A complete corruption sweep or completely random labels is not required to test these components.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits the training-dynamics contribution: under restrictive synthetic-data assumptions, clean margin determines benign, harmful or no overfitting, and the analysis distinguishes an early clean-fitting phase from later corrupted-point fitting or suppression. The authors emphasize limitations from near-orthogonal noise, rank-one signal and noise-distribution assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a theoretical two-layer ReLU network trained by full-batch gradient descent with hinge loss on synthetic linearly separable data containing flipped labels. The claim concerns standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods on image datasets with random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper shows outcomes change with the clean-data margin γ: theorems identify benign-overfitting, harmful-overfitting, and no-overfitting regimes. In Figure 2, clean-point fitting can fail when γ is small and n is large under fixed dimension d.
record.problems: The authors identify a restrictive data model: near-orthogonal noise, a rank-one signal, and additional noise-distribution assumptions. The theorems require specific conditions on model and data hyperparameters. Numerical simulations use synthetic data; Figure 2's outcomes are presented as heatmaps without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional study results bearing on the listed versions were identified. Prior-work results cited in the paper were excluded.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling with chance test error under unchanged standard architectures and stochastic training settings.
Training-time ratios against true-label training and convergence slowing as corruption increases. The shared upper bounds on termination time do not establish either comparison.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A corruption sweep from none to all and steadily increasing test error toward chance; experiments instead vary margin and sample size at fixed corruption.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, augmentation and removing these regularizers.
Learning order on natural datasets, completely random-label training, and generality beyond the restricted synthetic model and analyzed hinge-loss dynamics.

missing.what: A separate theoretical dynamics row establishing early clean fitting followed by corrupted-label fitting: clean loss ≤ 1/3 at T1, corrupted loss bounded near 1, and subsequent small clean loss while corrupt points reach zero loss.
missing.locator: Abstract; Lemma 3.4; Appendix C.3, Lemma C.7; Appendix C.4, Lemmas C.9 and C.12

record.verdict_notes: Zero hinge loss guarantees correct classification, but nonzero hinge loss alone need not imply classification error. R3 additionally specifies zero network output on corrupted points. No numerical values were inferred from unavailable figure images. This study is not an original source for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, chance test error, and unchanged standard architecture and stochastic training settings.
No comparison of training time for random versus true labels, or convergence time across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
No sweep from zero to complete random corruption establishing perfect training fit and steadily rising test error.
No test of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
The paper analyzes clean and corrupted labels in phases, but does not test random labels or establish the claim's stated comparison for real versus random labels.

conditions.value: 2n linearly separable synthetic binary examples; k corrupted points per sign
C log(n/δ)/d ≤ γ ≤ cn−1; ρ ≤ cγ
full-batch gradient descent; sufficiently small step-size η
at least 1 − δ over dataset and initialization

rows.measure: training hinge loss and test misclassification probability
rows.value: All training points have zero loss; generalization error ≤ exp(−cdγ²); training terminates by Tend ≤ Cn/η.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − δ; constants C and c are unspecified.
rows.note: The result concerns a structured synthetic data model with a minority of flipped labels, not completely random labels.
rows.check: Theorem 3.1 establishes perfect fitting of clean and flipped labels with low test error under its margin assumptions. Correct the margin lower bound to C√(log(n/δ)/d). This endpoint row does not establish a corruption-response curve or learning order.
